item.title: South Africa’s Market Rebound Shows Its Economic Potential Is Real
item.description: President Donald Trump's diatribe against South Africa less than a month into his second term, when he dissolved United States Agency for International Development (USAID) programs over his dubious understanding of the country’s land appropriation laws, couldn't have been better timed as a contrary indicator.
item.dc:creator: Matthew A. Winkler

item.title: Can Japan Say Goodbye to Middle Eastern Oil?
item.description: Among the world’s top fuel-consuming nations, Japan is the most energy insecure. Its import-dependency ratios are scary: It buys overseas 99.9% of the oil it needs; 99.7% of the coal; and 97.8% of the natural gas. So Tokyo springs into action after every major energy shock to reassess its supply sources, making it a bellwether of global trends. The direction it’s signaling this time? Run away from the Middle East.
item.dc:creator: Javier Blas

item.title: Hedge Funds Moving to Athens Could Be a Heavy Loss for City of London
item.description: When Alpha Bank’s Konstantinos Sarafopoulos returned home to Greece in 2021 after more than 20 years in the UK — 17 of them spent at JPMorgan Chase & Co. — he found a changed landscape. Recession and austerity were gone, attractive tax packages were being rolled out and bureaucracy was being eased by digitalization. “Not so positive was the traffic,” Sarafopoulos, the lender’s chief risk officer, tells me. “But that’s maybe testament to the country’s recent success.”
item.dc:creator: Lionel Laurent

item.title: UK Politics: Tony Blair Old Master of British Politics Is Worth a Listen
item.description: Tony Blair is not just any backseat driver. He is the UK’s and the ruling Labour Party’s most successful living politician, the winner of three decisive general elections. So when he talks, Andy Burnham needs to listen, even if the prime minister in the driving seat dislikes what he hears.
item.dc:creator: Martin Ivens

item.title: Around the World in 80 Days? There's a Token for That
item.description: Maybe Mark Zuckerberg spoiled it for us seven years ago. Ever since the Silicon Valley czar proposed a new global currency that could meet the “daily financial needs of billions of people,” we imagined that the money best suited for humans and AI agents in the 21st century could only be minted privately — with blockchain technology.
item.dc:creator: Andy Mukherjee

item.title: Trump's UN Bluster Didn't Scare Xi, Putin or Iran
item.description: Donald Trump loves playing the tough guy. The president postured from the podium at the United Nations this week. He threatened to send the Iranian regime “into hell”; he gloated about his appropriation of Venezuelan oil, declaring, “to the victor belong the spoils.”
item.dc:creator: Hal Brands

item.title: The Irony of the GOP Buying So Many NFL Ads Ahead of Midterms
item.description: Republican politicians have repeatedly tried to pick fights with the National Football League. In just the past two years, Speaker Mike Johnson and others derided the choice of Bad Bunny as a Super Bowl halftime entertainer, while Senator Tommy Tuberville targeted the Minnesota Vikings’ male cheerleaders — accusing the league of wanting “to put gender in sports.” And who can forget President Donald Trump’s demand that the Washington Commanders change their name back to a racial slur?
item.dc:creator: Adam Minter
